title: Christopher Cock’s five-draw telescope
summary: Cock’s 1673 five-draw telescope was intended for land viewing and has three lenses.
limit: A clear landmark in this exercise does not show that the historical tube was made for astronomy.
firstAction: Line up the paper tube with the near quay post.
firstReading: The slot holds the near quay post and the far beacon drops out.
secondAction: Turn the paper tube to the far beacon.
secondReading: The far beacon fills the slot. The quay post remains off the strip.
returnEvidence: On the Bell Archive trial, the waiting carrier sees the beacon from the high window. At the low entrance their quay post is the usable bearing.
hang: Hang the near quay-post frame at the low entrance.
desk: Return both sightlines to the staffed frame.

title: Caroline Herschel’s reflecting telescope
summary: The museum dates several parts across 1795–1816 and considers the surviving Newtonian telescope to have been assembled with parts William made for Caroline.
limit: The catalogue’s reconstruction of assembly does not date every part to one year.
firstAction: Put the reading tube and accessory box in separate cradles.
firstReading: The long cradle holds the black tube. The small tray holds eyepieces and fittings.
secondAction: Swing the study frame to reveal the separate component tags.
secondReading: One tag names the earlier optical work. The fittings retain the broader interval.
returnEvidence: At the Bell Archive, the dismantled practice mount needs a parts list. The waiting reader can hang a two-part sketch while the steward checks the uncertain order of assembly.
hang: Hang the separate tube and eyepiece cradles on the public clip.
desk: Leave the two-component comparison with the steward.

title: William Herschel’s reflecting telescope for William Watson
summary: Herschel made this Newtonian telescope for William Watson in Bath. Surviving accessories include a pamphlet of instructions.
limit: The pamphlet records intended operation. It does not establish which observations Watson made.
firstAction: Set the model’s direction guide by the empty stand.
firstReading: The conversion marks can still be read when no sight line is set.
secondAction: Move the study stand to the drawn sight line.
secondReading: The bright spot lands on the viewing card and the directions remain in their separate clip.
returnEvidence: At the archive, the reader can compare the settings against the surviving manual record. A visit for instructions and a visit to verify an observation need different trays.
hang: Put the operating route with the equipment sketch at the rail.
desk: Keep the rule and observation placeholders together at the staffed table.

title: William Herschel’s filar micrometer
summary: This eyepiece micrometer used fixed and movable wires for angular measurements. The catalogue records missing threads on the screw.
limit: The scale can survive after a moving part that made it usable has been lost.
firstAction: Bring the loose paper wire to the first edge of the drawn object.
firstReading: The wire just touches the edge. The fixed wire remains at the other side.
secondAction: Slide the loose wire to the larger drawing’s edge.
secondReading: The wire separation doubles on the same printed scale.
returnEvidence: At the archive, a volunteer brings the object inventory over on a separate strip. The missing screw threads stay marked while readers test the paper reconstruction.
hang: Clip up the two measured paper widths with a separate missing-part note.
desk: Leave the operation and the missing-thread inventory together at the staffed table.

title: Girolamo della Volpaia’s armillary sphere
summary: This signed model surrounds a terrestrial globe with interlocking rings and uses an Earth-centred arrangement.
limit: Tracing a path on the model describes the model’s construction. It does not settle how bodies move in the sky.
firstAction: Slide the bright bead round the outside ring.
firstReading: The path returns to the side from which it started. The Earth card stays fixed in the middle.
secondAction: Move the viewer’s footmark outside the model.
secondReading: The path still closes. From the other side the drawing reads in the reverse order.
returnEvidence: At the archive, visitors can repeat the ring path. A second clip identifies the fixed centre as part of the model’s design.
hang: Hang the repeatable ring path and its fixed-centre key.
desk: Keep the two viewpoints together on the staffed table.

title: John Russell’s Moon globe
summary: Russell’s globe models the Moon’s Earth-facing side. Its libration stand includes a smaller Earth globe.
limit: A feature brought into view in this model does not supply coverage of every far-side feature.
firstAction: Tip the small shoe on the grey paper Moon model towards Earth.
firstReading: A striped edge comes into the viewing circle from the left.
secondAction: Tip the shoe away from the Earth marker.
secondReading: The striped edge slips out of the circle and a seam appears at the other edge.
returnEvidence: The Bell Archive lends an Earth marker and two edge sleeves. The steward can keep the off-frame strip available without claiming it has been mapped.
hang: Hang the two observed edges with a blank for the rest.
desk: Leave the Earth marker and both edge sleeves on the staffed table.

title: Jeremiah Sisson’s mural arc
summary: This signed brass and iron arc was installed at Richmond in 1770. Its divided scale covers 142 degrees and the fittings are incomplete.
limit: The scale’s size is documented. It cannot supply an observation outside the remaining fittings.
firstAction: Clip the ruler to the study wall inside the arc ends.
firstReading: The reference ray crosses a marked division.
secondAction: Move the ray past the last marked division.
secondReading: The ray reaches blank paper. There is no division to read at the wall edge.
returnEvidence: The archive reader has marked a blank beyond the study arc. Another reader can handle the movable ray to see why it remains blank.
hang: Clip the marked reach and the blank end together by the wall.
desk: Leave the measuring arc and adjustable ray with the steward.

title: Kew Observatory’s short-period vertical seismometer
summary: The Kew short-period instrument recorded the vertical component. Two other instruments recorded horizontal components.
limit: An empty vertical trace cannot establish the absence of motion in the horizontal directions.
firstAction: Raise the practice deck straight up a notch.
firstReading: The vertical paper trace moves across one printed line.
secondAction: Slide the practice deck along the table without raising it.
secondReading: The vertical paper trace stays on its line. The horizontal witness tag changes position.
returnEvidence: The archive late shift can check which motion the narrow trace can see. Its horizontal witness card stays on a separate peg.
hang: Hang the trace next to the independent side-slide witness.
desk: Set the two-axis practice deck at the staffed table.

title: Willmore Mark IV borehole seismometer no. 5509
summary: The three-component Willmore Mark IV borehole instrument is serial number 5509. Sensonics made it at Chesham in 1979.
limit: Three channels plotted together need their direction keys to preserve what each trace represents.
firstAction: Slot the three coloured direction slips into their separate grooves.
firstReading: The vertical, side and forward tracks have separate origins on this practice panel.
secondAction: Overlay the copies without covering their keys.
secondReading: Two peaks share a paper position but the different direction tags remain visible.
returnEvidence: At the archive, two readers can use a keyed overlay to compare positions while naming the separate practice axes.
hang: Hang all three tracks with the axis tags projecting.
desk: Keep the overlay and original direction slips on the staffed table.

title: Daniel Quare’s portable barometer
summary: Quare made this portable mercury barometer. The museum describes Derham’s separate 1697 experiments using a Quare barometer.
limit: The object record connects the design to the experiment. It does not identify this particular specimen as the instrument used by Derham.
firstAction: Mount two printed pressure readings beside the same named location.
firstReading: Both figures belong to the same site at the ground footmark.
secondAction: Move one printed reading to the upper footmark and keep its own date tag.
secondReading: The figures still differ, and now the board names two distinct positions.
returnEvidence: At the archive, the source divider keeps this accession’s history apart from Derham’s reported use of a Quare instrument. Nothing liquid is handled.
hang: Hang the named places beside the printed readings.
desk: Keep the accession and experiment records on the open staffed table.

title: Birmingham & Derby Junction Railway guard’s timepiece no. 1
summary: George Littlewort’s guard’s timepiece no. 1 has a circular Roman-numeral face in a rectangular case.
limit: One guard’s timepiece cannot establish a universal railway timekeeping practice.
firstAction: Align the guard’s study dial with the platform slip.
firstReading: Both read the same mark on this model’s arrival.
secondAction: Turn the model platform dial forward but leave the guard’s copy still.
secondReading: The platform has moved. The old reading remains with the named guard’s slip.
returnEvidence: At the archive, one hook records the physical timepiece, while its neighbouring hook takes the local test of how two clocks were read.
hang: Hang the guard’s reading beside a separately signed platform slip.
desk: Keep the dial and two changing views at the staffed table.

title: Willem Janszoon Blaeu’s celestial globe
summary: The stars are plotted on the outside of this celestial globe made at Amsterdam in 1603.
limit: A pattern read from outside the model and a sky seen from within have different viewpoints.
firstAction: Put the paper constellation against the outside of the globe.
firstReading: The paper star pair reads east marker, bright mark, west marker.
secondAction: Turn the view sleeve to face outward from inside the study circle.
secondReading: The markers appear in the opposite left-to-right order. The pattern has not been rearranged.
returnEvidence: At the archive, a star-spotter uses the inside strip. The outside globe view stays available for anyone comparing the two.
hang: Hang the inside and outside strips with their own footmarks.
desk: Store both strips with the rotating frame at the staffed table.

title: Dubois’s Cassini-type altazimuth quadrant
summary: The catalogue attributes this brass example to Dubois. The type uses two arcs to read horizontal and vertical angles.
limit: An elevation on one scale alone leaves the horizontal direction unspecified.
firstAction: Raise the sight marker on its vertical study arc.
firstReading: The height mark rises two divisions and the base direction stays still.
secondAction: Pivot the lower ring while keeping the height mark in place.
secondReading: The direction changes three divisions with no change on the height strip.
returnEvidence: At the archive, the caller needs a pair of coordinates to locate the practice object. Readers can replay both independent motions.
hang: Hang both angle strips with their separately named zero marks.
desk: Keep both motions on the staffed table with the finder.

title: Giovanni Battista Amici’s wooden telescope mount
summary: Amici’s wooden frame supported a telescope while permitting limited horizontal movement so an observer could hold a target briefly in view.
limit: A short clear view does not mean the mount follows the whole sky.
firstAction: Slide the practice twin-star marker across the fixed view.
firstReading: Both stars leave the slot before the study line ends.
secondAction: Turn the frame to its second stop while the marker passes.
secondReading: The pair stays visible longer and drops out at the final mark.
returnEvidence: At the Bell Archive, the reader walks the two observation windows. The record keeps the final blank after the turning mount reaches its stop.
hang: Hang both timed sight slots and their endpoints.
desk: Keep the rolling star strip and mount at the staffed table.

title: Chérubin d’Orléans’s binocular telescope
summary: This wooden instrument contains two telescopic paths. Parts are missing from the inner tubes.
limit: Two drawn lines of sight explain the arrangement. They do not show that the surviving instrument can still form its original two views.
firstAction: Set the left paper channel across the pair of sights.
firstReading: The left slot shows the near notch and the distant pin.
secondAction: Move the cover to the incomplete right path.
secondReading: The drawing leaves an open gap at the incomplete part. The nearby pin has no registered view on that channel.
returnEvidence: At the archive, visitors can compare the proposed paired path with a record of the surviving sections.
hang: Hang the visible ray beside the right-path gap.
desk: Keep both tube sections and the missing-parts slip with the steward.

title: Galileo’s objective lens with Vittorio Crosten’s frame
summary: Museo Galileo dates the objective lens and its later frame separately. The lens was accidentally cracked after its observing use.
limit: The frame supplies a later custody date. It does not date the observations or explain their evidence by itself.
firstAction: Rest the paper lens in the unframed study cradle.
firstReading: The broken line belongs to the lens. The observing date goes in the lens tray.
secondAction: Place the same study lens inside the paper frame.
secondReading: The glass edge is in the same place and the display frame now has a separate dated tag.
returnEvidence: At the archive, the loan slip has one line for optical use and one for mounting. A visitor can read either date without turning it into the whole story.
hang: Hang the observation and framing dates on separate hooks.
desk: Keep the whole custody handover with the steward.

title: Selva workshop’s incomplete Gregorian telescope
summary: The incomplete telescope is signed by Domenico Selva but may be the work of his son Lorenzo. Its secondary mirror is missing.
limit: The signed name does not resolve who personally made the instrument.
firstAction: Set the signature slip next to the remaining mirror disc.
firstReading: The name remains legible. The model’s optical path stops at the empty secondary position.
secondAction: Put the 1761 account beside the signature in a second holder.
secondReading: Lorenzo’s account leaves both maker attributions open.
returnEvidence: At the archive, a reader can see why the signature remains valuable without closing the maker question. The empty mirror bracket stays in the drawing.
hang: Hang the signature beside the separate workshop account.
desk: Keep the optical frame and both custody records on the staffed table.

title: Reichenbach workshop’s repeating circle
summary: This rotating telescope measures angles and uses a repetition system for precise altitude measurement. The objective is signed by Fraunhofer.
limit: The repeatable reading describes the instrument’s method, not a guarantee that any particular alignment was accurate.
firstAction: Make one paper turn from the zero notch.
firstReading: The practice drum accumulates four divisions on the altitude run.
secondAction: Repeat the same turn twice, using the same starting notch.
secondReading: The accumulated mark reaches twelve divisions across three equal turns.
returnEvidence: At the archive, a reader can replay the three turns and see why a fixed zero marker must travel with the answer.
hang: Hang the accumulation with its starting notch and number of turns.
desk: Keep the repeatable circle and zero marker with the steward.

title: Florence workshop’s two-telescope level
summary: The level has two opposed telescopes and a plumb-line reference. It was built in the Florence museum workshop and probably designed by Fontana.
limit: A matching line on one side does not show both sides share a horizontal reference.
firstAction: Bring the west paper sight to the cross-mark.
firstReading: The left mark is level but the right marker still sits low.
secondAction: Put the common plumb marker alongside both sight lines.
secondReading: Both can be adjusted against the same vertical mark in the study frame.
returnEvidence: At the archive, the matched cross-marks are only useful with the shared plumb mark still visible. The creator slip preserves the design attribution.
hang: Hang both lines with the common plumb mark and qualified attribution.
desk: Keep the opposed sights and loose targets on the staffed table.

title: Galgano Gori’s mobile eyepiece mount
summary: Gori’s signed mount moved the eyepiece across the focal plane and could turn about an axis parallel to the optical axis.
limit: Following a target with a moving eyepiece is not evidence that the target itself changed course.
firstAction: Slide the eyepiece marker after the passing study star.
firstReading: The dot stays in the view as the eyepiece slides. The fixed star track is unchanged.
secondAction: Return the eyepiece to the start while the dot continues.
secondReading: The dot slips out of the window at the marked edge.
returnEvidence: At the archive, a reader moves the viewing window separately from the paper target. The dot’s path and the operator’s movement get separate lines.
hang: Hang the fixed track above the moving-window strip.
desk: Keep the eyepiece slide and target track with the steward.

title: Giovanni Battista Amici’s dipleidoscope
summary: Amici’s instrument uses two images whose overlap can indicate true local noon when the axis is placed in the meridian plane.
limit: Overlap on a misaligned study plate does not by itself establish local noon. The playable aid is flat printed paper.
firstAction: Bring the two printed discs together on the loose study card.
firstReading: The discs overlap even though the base direction has not been checked.
secondAction: Align the printed base with the separate meridian mark and repeat.
secondReading: The two discs overlap at the meridian mark on the checked paper model.
returnEvidence: At the archive, the two overlap strips look alike at a glance. The named alignment goes with the reading where the next visitor can repeat it.
hang: Hang the direction key with the two overlapping strips.
desk: Keep the printed image model and separate meridian mark at the staffed table.

title: Cardinal Bessarion’s astrolabe
summary: The astrolabe’s inscription names Bessarion and a maker called John, thought to be Regiomontanus. Its reverse is engraved with an angel.
limit: The patron’s name is secure on the object. Identifying the maker with a particular astronomer remains an attribution.
firstAction: Place the patron’s inscription in the named custody slot.
firstReading: Bessarion’s name remains attached to the instrument rather than its reading.
secondAction: Turn the study disc and lift the separate maker tab.
secondReading: The maker is named John. The proposed identification sits on a loose clip.
returnEvidence: At the archive, visitors can read the naming evidence without treating a scholarly identification as an inscription.
hang: Hang the inscription and proposed identity on two labelled clips.
desk: Keep the reversible model and both notes at the staffed table.

title: Muhammad Zaman’s planispheric astrolabe
summary: The Met attributes this signed portable astrolabe to Mashhad in Iran and distinguishes practical timekeeping from more precise astronomical observation.
limit: The reading on a practice disc cannot set the angular precision of the historical original.
firstAction: Bring the broad practice pointer into the hour interval.
firstReading: The marker is visible inside one interval from the low rail.
secondAction: Move the pointer within the interval by one small division.
secondReading: Both positions give the same broad interval at that viewpoint.
returnEvidence: At the archive, the reader can use the broad interval to plan a meeting. The divided diagram at the staffed table shows why a finer reading stays open.
hang: Hang the broad time band with its usable precision.
desk: Keep the magnified division plate and broad interval at the staffed table.

title: Petrus Apianus’s Astronomicum Caesareum
summary: This book models celestial positions with rotating printed discs and includes Apianus’s observations on the comet of 1531.
limit: Moving the book’s disc illustrates a procedure. A separate account supports what Apianus reported observing.
firstAction: Turn the practice paper wheel until two markers meet.
firstReading: The movable disc supplies a predicted position aligned with the printed index.
secondAction: Raise the second clip with the handwritten study observation.
secondReading: It has its own date and record place. The wheel has not moved.
returnEvidence: At the archive, the reader can rerun the wheel from its starting mark while the dated observation remains separately visible.
hang: Hang the prediction and dated sighting on different rails.
desk: Keep the rotating wheel and recorded sighting together at the staffed table.

title: Nuremberg mirror clock
summary: The Met distinguishes the attributed movement, probable stem-and-foot designer, and ornamental source behind this mirror clock’s case band.
limit: An attribution for one part cannot stand in for the maker of every part.
firstAction: Put the case band and movement in two labelled study places.
firstReading: The clock movement has its own attribution. The case band points to a design source.
secondAction: Place the stem and foot template on their third peg.
secondReading: The maker label now has three parts, including a visibly qualified third attribution.
returnEvidence: At the archive, a reader can follow the recorded role of the part they need. All three remain related by one catalogue number.
hang: Hang the three labelled part silhouettes along the accessible rail.
desk: Keep the case, movement and parts table ready for assisted comparison.

title: Wall clock and thermometer with Sèvres plaques
summary: This Paris wall piece combines a clock and a thermometer and incorporates porcelain by Sèvres with decoration credited to Dodin.
limit: Co-location on one case does not give time and temperature the same unit or maker role.
firstAction: Move the upper model hand through one time division.
firstReading: The hour ticks forward. The separate temperature strip stays fixed.
secondAction: Move the temperature marker while the clock hand holds its place.
secondReading: The temperature moves one division on a separate scale.
returnEvidence: The archive reader can find both measurements in a glance, with the signs and credits kept in separate boxes.
hang: Hang one combined board with distinctly titled measures and roles.
desk: Keep the separate movable measures in the staffed model.

title: Paulus Reinman’s diptych sundial
summary: The dated object is a two-part ivory and brass portable sundial by Paulus Reinman.
limit: The look of the closed object does not show whether a usable reading position is available.
firstAction: Close the hinged paper study plate flat.
firstReading: The second panel covers the study shadow lines.
secondAction: Open the practice plate to its marked stop.
secondReading: The lines are visible together. The hinge angle is now named on the study stand.
returnEvidence: At the archive, the public desk can show the open study view, or the steward can let readers compare both positions of the hinge.
hang: Hang the open view with the drawn hinge stop.
desk: Keep the folding model with the steward so both views can be repeated.

title: French combined portable astronomical dial
summary: The Met notes that its calendar disc is calibrated to the Julian calendar. France adopted the Gregorian calendar in 1582.
limit: A printed date on the calibrated disc must keep its calendar convention with it.
firstAction: Rotate the Julian study band to the marked date slot.
firstReading: The number lines up with the Julian tag inside the practice disc.
secondAction: Lay the separately named Gregorian band over the case without converting it.
secondReading: The printed number looks familiar. It sits in a differently named calendar column.
returnEvidence: At the archive, readers can keep the printed date with its calendar name. The conversion line is left empty pending a separate comparison.
hang: Hang the two calendar headings with the retained source date.
desk: Keep the date disc, headings and separate conversion space at the staffed table.

title: Claude Dunod’s portable compass dial
summary: The 1714 portable compass dial is made of gilded brass and silver and is catalogued as horology.
limit: A turn of a practice plate may change a dial position even while the external direction stays put.
firstAction: Set the paper dial next to the fixed north stripe.
firstReading: The practice reading is on the inner scale while the north stripe has its own place.
secondAction: Rotate the inner number band beneath the stationary stripe.
secondReading: A different number sits under the same direction stripe.
returnEvidence: At the archive, two witnesses stand one by the dial and one by the direction mark. Their views answer different questions about the same turn.
hang: Hang the fixed direction above the turning scale.
desk: Keep the sliding dial at the staffed table with its direction key.

title: Apollo 8 Earthrise frame AS08-14-2383
summary: NASA identifies a telephoto view from Apollo 8. Earth appears about five degrees above the lunar horizon.
limit: The apparent angle is tied to the camera position and view. It does not give Earth’s physical size.
firstAction: Clip the Earth marker in the narrow lunar-horizon study frame.
firstReading: The Earth marker sits about five divisions above the horizon on this exercise ruler.
secondAction: Pull back the paper viewing window without moving either mark.
secondReading: More of the scene enters the frame. The two marks have not changed their angle.
returnEvidence: At the archive, visitors can compare narrow framing with a wider study view. The angle and the crop have different captions.
hang: Hang the narrow frame alongside the preserved horizon marker.
desk: Keep both viewing windows open at the staffed table.

title: Apollo 17 Earth frame AS17-148-22727
summary: The Apollo 17 crew could photograph a view extending down to the Antarctic ice cap. Much of the southern part is covered by cloud.
limit: NASA lists the crew. This record neither names a specific photographer nor supplies ground detail concealed by clouds.
firstAction: Set the wide paper window across the study disc.
firstReading: The coast and ice-cap tags fit on the visible disc.
secondAction: Move the clear weather sleeve to expose the cloud mask.
secondReading: The marked coast still shows. The masked area supplies no new land detail.
returnEvidence: At the archive, visitors can point out which areas the photograph allows them to name. Unseen ground stays in the cloud slot.
hang: Hang the coastline and the cloud limit on the same frame.
desk: Keep the mask in the staffed window so visitors can repeat the check.

title: Viking 1’s first Mars surface photograph
summary: Viking 1’s camera no. 2 took the first Mars surface photograph shortly after landing. Part of the lander’s second footpad appears at the right.
limit: A feature near the pad may come from landing activity. A single early frame cannot separate every surface process.
firstAction: Clip the lander pad outline over the right edge of the study frame.
firstReading: The manufactured pad now has its own marker, away from the natural rocks in the middle.
secondAction: Lay the possible landing-disturbance strip by the near ground.
secondReading: The study mark bounds a place for comparison. It does not name one proven cause.
returnEvidence: At the archive, the frame can guide a repeat comparison of disturbed and more distant ground. The possible cause keeps its qualifier.
hang: Hang the pad marker with a plainly qualified ground tag.
desk: Keep both ground views on the staffed frame for a repeat inspection.

title: Enhanced contrast release of the first Mariner 4 Mars image
summary: NASA records this as an enhanced contrast version of Mariner 4’s first Mars image released in 1965.
limit: Changing visible contrast can change what a viewer detects. It does not create a new flyby or a second independent exposure.
firstAction: Put the low-contrast paper strip below the grid.
firstReading: One faint boundary nearly disappears against its field.
secondAction: Slide the higher-contrast copy above the same grid without shifting it.
secondReading: The edge looks clearer at the same positions. No additional marks were sampled.
returnEvidence: At the archive, two copies can share a source date while keeping a separate line for later processing.
hang: Hang the clearest boundary with both dates in view.
desk: Keep both contrast strips and their common grid on the staffed frame.

title: Cassini mosaic The Day the Earth Smiled
summary: Cassini photographed a panorama from Saturn’s shadow. The mosaic includes Saturn, parts of its rings, several moons and distant Earth.
limit: This geometry is a particular camera view. It does not make a photograph of the same quality possible from any direction.
firstAction: Set the paper camera behind Saturn’s shadow line.
firstReading: The bright centre is covered and the small background marker can be set within the study window.
secondAction: Move the viewing cursor to the unshielded position on the plan.
secondReading: The glare tag crosses the study window. This paper path keeps the marked recording position distinct.
returnEvidence: At the archive, a diagram traces why this shot had a special viewing position. The image record and the shadow drawing retain different labels.
hang: Hang the selected view with the shadow position keyed.
desk: Keep the camera-view overlay and path plan at the staffed table.

title: Hubble sequence of Phobos beside Mars
summary: Hubble recorded Phobos in 13 separate exposures over 22 minutes while observing Mars.
limit: The frame sequence traces part of the orbit. The gaps contain no separately observed position from this series.
firstAction: Slide the numbered exposure strips into time order.
firstReading: The white dot moves between strips. The sequence keeps its separate exposure marks.
secondAction: Lift the cover over the gap between two strips.
secondReading: No exposure appears under the cover. The curved connection is a drawn aid.
returnEvidence: At the archive, a visitor can track the observed dots, with the connecting arc printed faintly under a different key.
hang: Hang the observed exposure marks with blank intervals.
desk: Keep the ordered frames and optional path overlay with the steward.

title: Fifty Years of Mars Imaging: Mariner 4 to HiRISE
summary: This NASA comparison compiles changing image resolutions over one site. The HiRISE view covers the smallest area at the finest scale shown.
limit: The 2017 compilation presents several observations from different times and footprints. More local detail can mean less surrounding context.
firstAction: Set down the broad Mariner comparison window.
firstReading: The broad window locates the site but the tiny study boulders merge.
secondAction: Fit the narrow high-detail HiRISE window over the same marked site.
secondReading: The small blocks separate. The surrounding terrain has moved out of that window.
returnEvidence: At the archive, a runner needs the large map to find the site. The detailed slip goes with the person checking the local blocks.
hang: Hang a wide locator with the small detailed window outlined.
desk: Keep the full set of window sizes at the staffed comparison table.
